13:I[9227,["809","static/chunks/809-a74e063132212cdb.js","714","static/chunks/714-e58065388e176c6d.js","690","static/chunks/app/verse/%5Bid%5D/page-179c881197ecc822.js"],"default"]
8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":19,"verseId":2,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Time","totalVerses":6,"verseData":{"id":"v19_2","number":2,"title":"Without Pre-Existence, How Can There Be Inherent Dependence?","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"If the present and future Did not exist there, How could the present and future Be dependent upon it?"},"philosophy":{"insight":"The second horn: if present and future did NOT pre-exist in the past (avoiding v.1's absurdity), then how could they INHERENTLY depend on it? Inherent dependence requires a connection — but between what? The past (which exists) and the present/future (which don't yet exist in the past). You can't have an inherent relation to something non-existent.","madhyamaka":"If pratyutpanna and anāgata did NOT exist (na vidyete) in the atīta, then their inherent dependence (apekṣā) on the past is impossible. Inherent apekṣā requires both relata to exist. If the dependent (present/future) doesn't exist where the depended-upon (past) exists, no inherent connection can be established.","quantum":"Retrocausality problem: in standard QM, the future doesn't \"exist\" to influence the past. If future measurements don't pre-exist, how can they affect past preparations? Some interpretations (like the two-state vector formalism) suggest retrocausal influence, but this remains deeply controversial — paralleling v.2's puzzle about connecting non-existent future to existing past.","bridge":"Both v.2 and the retrocausality problem ask: how can something that doesn't yet exist be connected to what does? QM: how does a future measurement affect a past state? V.2: how does a non-existent present/future depend on an existing past? Both: the connection between existent and non-existent is problematic.","accessible":"How can something that doesn't exist yet depend on something that does? It's like saying \"the child depends on the parent\" BEFORE the child is born. The relationship requires both parties to exist. If the present/future don't exist in the past, the dependency can't be established.","twoTruths":"Conventionally: we say the future \"depends on\" the present — and this works. Ultimately: the inherent connection between a present existence and a not-yet-existent future can't be established. Convention works; inherent connection doesn't.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying the past can't influence the future. Conventional causal conditioning through time is affirmed. What's denied is an INHERENT connection between the self-existing past and the not-yet-existing present/future."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Retrocausality Problem — Connecting Present to Non-Existent Future","score":58,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"Retrocausality: how can future measurements (not yet existing) affect past states? Like v.2: how can present/future (not existing in the past) depend on the past? Both: the connection between existent and non-existent is problematic.","caveat":"Retrocausality is a quantum foundations debate. V.2 is a Madhyamaka philosophical argument. The parallel is about connecting what exists to what doesn't yet exist."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"The Past gate exists solidly. Present and Future gates are ghostly/non-existent. A line tries to connect them — but fails. You can't draw an inherent connection between what exists (past) and what doesn't yet exist (present/future).","educationalGoal":"User sees that inherent dependence requires both terms to exist. If present/future don't exist in the past, the inherent connection can't be drawn."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Why can't you have an inherent relation to something non-existent?","a":"An inherent relation is part of the ESSENCE of the relata. Essences must exist to have relationships. If the present doesn't exist in the past, it has no essence there to be related. An inherent connection requires BOTH sides to inherently exist at the same \"place.\" No existence → no essence → no inherent relation.","realLifeExample":"You can't sign a contract with someone who doesn't exist yet (like your future grandchild). The contract requires both parties to exist. Similarly: inherent dependence requires both past and present/future to co-exist."},{"q":"Isn't this just Hume's problem of causation?","a":"Similar but deeper. Hume: we can't OBSERVE the necessary connection between cause and effect. Nāgārjuna: the INHERENT connection can't even be coherently CONCEIVED. Hume doubts whether we can know the connection exists. Nāgārjuna shows the inherent connection is logically impossible.","realLifeExample":"Hume: \"I can't see the glue between the billiard balls.\" Nāgārjuna: \"There CAN'T be inherent glue — the concept itself is incoherent.\" Deeper: not just epistemic doubt but ontological impossibility."},{"q":"How does v.2 follow from v.1?","a":"V.1: IF present/future pre-exist in the past → they're not really present/future (absurd). V.2: IF they DON'T pre-exist → they can't inherently depend on the past (no connection). V.1 and v.2 are two horns of a dilemma: pre-exist (absurd) or don't pre-exist (no connection). Both options fail.","realLifeExample":"Either the surprise was already \"in\" the plan (v.1 — then it's not a surprise) or it wasn't in the plan (v.2 — then how did it come from the plan?). The dilemma exposes the problem of inherent planning for surprises."},{"q":"What is the conventional solution?","a":"EMPTY dependence: the present depends on the past CONVENTIONALLY (through conditions, not through inherent connection). Empty causes produce empty effects. The connection is real but not inherent — it's a dependent designation, not a self-existing relationship.","realLifeExample":"A child depends on their parents — but not INHERENTLY (not as part of the child's eternal essence). The dependence is real but conventional: it arose from conditions and could change. V.2's problem only arises for INHERENT dependence; conventional dependence works fine."},{"q":"Does quantum mechanics face a similar problem?","a":"Yes — the \"problem of time\" in quantum gravity: (1) The Schrödinger equation describes evolution IN time, but (2) the Wheeler-DeWitt equation (quantum gravity) suggests time doesn't fundamentally exist. How can you have temporal evolution without fundamental time? Like v.2: how can you have temporal dependence without inherent temporal connection?","realLifeExample":"Running a race where the track doesn't fundamentally exist — it's constructed as you run. Quantum gravity: time is constructed through physical processes, not a pre-existing container. V.2: temporal dependence is conventional, not inherent."},{"q":"What is the philosophical significance of the dilemma?","a":"The dilemma (vv.1-2) is exhaustive for inherent dependence: either the dependent pre-exists in its basis (v.1 — absurd) or it doesn't (v.2 — no connection). Since these are the only options for inherent dependence, inherent temporal dependence is impossible. This doesn't destroy temporal dependence — it reveals it as empty (conventional, not inherent).","deeper":"V.2 completes the dilemma opened by v.1. Together, they show that INHERENT temporal dependence faces an irresolvable choice: co-existence (which collapses temporal distinction) or non-co-existence (which prevents the connection). This is the same dilemma structure used in Ch.1 (conditions) and Ch.2 (motion): the hallmark of Mādhyamika analysis. The resolution is always the same: the relationship is CONVENTIONALLY real but ULTIMATELY empty. This applies to time just as it applies to causation and motion."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"Why can't present/future inherently depend on the past if they don't pre-exist in it?","options":["A) They can","B) Inherent dependence requires BOTH terms to exist. If present/future don't exist in the past, there's nothing there to establish the inherent connection.","C) The past doesn't exist","D) Only the present exists"],"correct":"B","explanation":"No existence → no essence → no inherent relation. Both sides of an inherent dependence must exist together."},"intermediate":{"question":"How do vv.1-2 form a dilemma?","options":["A) They don't","B) V.1: IF pre-exist → times collapse (absurd). V.2: IF don't pre-exist → no inherent connection possible. Either way, inherent temporal dependence fails. The two horns are exhaustive.","C) Only v.1 is a problem","D) Only v.2 is a problem"],"correct":"B","explanation":"Dilemma: pre-exist (absurd) OR don't pre-exist (no connection). Both options for inherent dependence fail."},"advanced":{"question":"How does the \"problem of time\" in quantum gravity parallel v.2?","options":["A) No parallel","B) Both ask: how can temporal relations exist if time isn't fundamental? QG: temporal evolution without fundamental time. V.2: temporal dependence without inherent temporal connection. Both: time is emergent/conventional, not fundamental/inherent.","C) QG proves time exists","D) V.2 proves time doesn't exist"],"correct":"B","explanation":"Both: temporal relations without fundamental time. Time is emergent (QG) / conventional (Madhyamaka), not inherent."}},"verseText":"If the present and future Did not exist there, How could the present and future Be dependent upon it?","madhyamakaConcept":"If pratyutpanna and anāgata did NOT exist (na vidyete) in the atīta, then their inherent dependence (apekṣā) on the past is impossible. Inherent apekṣā requires both relata to exist. If the dependent (present/future) doesn't exist where the depended-upon (past) exists, no inherent connection can be established.","quantumPhysicsParallel":"Retrocausality problem: in standard QM, the future doesn't \"exist\" to influence the past. If future measurements don't pre-exist, how can they affect past preparations?
